title: Thin-Slicing
subtitle: A sequence of tasks that change in tiny steps, so students extend their own understanding almost without noticing the difficulty rising.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Liljedahl, Building Thinking Classrooms (2020) · connects to Number Strings & the 5 Practices in this toolbelt.

blocks.text: A carefully ordered set of tasks where each one differs from the last by a **small variation**. Students work them in order at the whiteboards; the gentle increments let them notice patterns and build the next idea themselves.

From Liljedahl’s *Building Thinking Classrooms*, thin-slicing replaces “I do, we do, you do” with “you do, you do, you do — each a little harder.” Instead of the teacher demonstrating then assigning practice, the *sequence* does the teaching: a student who can do task 3 can almost always reach task 4, because the gap is deliberately thin.

They share a DNA — both use a designed sequence to lead thinking. **Number Strings** is an opener: a short mental-math string for fluency/strategy. **Thin-Slicing** is the Core version: a fuller set of tasks worked at the boards across the lesson, building toward a grade-level concept. If you can run a Number String, you already understand the engine.

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Tasks revealed one at a time, each a small step up
Groups noticing “oh, this is like the last one but…”
Most groups able to start each new slice
Increasing sophistication without a lecture
The teacher checking understanding between slices

no.title: We should *not* see
items: A big jump between tasks that strands most groups
A worksheet of unrelated problems
The teacher demonstrating the method first
All tasks shown at once (kills the noticing)
No consolidation of the big idea at the end

blocks.title: Slices too thick = the whole thing fails

blocks.text: The skill is in the *size of the step*. If task 4 is much harder than task 3, groups stall and you’re back to needing a lecture. When you see widespread stalling, your slices are too thick — add an intermediate task. Thin enough that nearly every group can take the next step on their own.

items: **The scaffolding is built into the sequence**, not bolted on for “some” students — everyone gets the same low-floor start and climbs the same gentle steps.
**Self-paced by group:** faster groups reach further slices; others go as far as they go — all on grade-level content, none on a watered-down sheet.
**Students arrive at the idea themselves**, which builds the disposition of students who’ve been told they “can’t do math.”

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: Liljedahl, Building Thinking Classrooms (2020) · Smith & Stein, 5 Practices (2011).

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson

It’s an Explore structure for Core Instruction — run at **vertical surfaces in random groups**, facilitated with the **5 Practices**, and closed with a consolidation. Reach for it when a concept builds naturally in steps (most procedural-conceptual topics do).
How to build a slice sequence

items: **Name the end point** — the grade-level task you want groups to reach.
**Write a low-floor opener** nearly every student can do immediately.
**Vary ONE thing at a time** between consecutive tasks — a number, a representation, a condition — so each step is small.
**Insert intermediate slices** wherever the jump feels big. When in doubt, thinner.
**Plan check-for-understanding questions** to pose between slices (and a sequel for fast groups).

blocks.text: A worked example: solving one-variable equations (IAS 7.EE / 8.EE)

Each step is thin enough that a group who solved the previous one can reason into the next — no lecture needed. The big idea (do the same to both sides; isolate the variable) emerges and gets named in consolidation.

items: **Random groups to the boards;** one marker each.
**Reveal one slice at a time.** When a group finishes, glance, then send the next task — verbally or on a card. Don’t post the whole list.
**Monitor** with your 5 Practices grid; note which strategies appear.
**Adjust live:** widespread stalling → insert a thinner slice on the fly.
**Consolidate:** select and sequence boards to name the big idea, not just the answers.

blocks.text: Your adopted curriculum’s problem sets are often *almost* a slice sequence already. Re-order them by difficulty, thin the big jumps, and deliver one at a time at the boards. That’s thin-slicing without writing tasks from scratch.

items: **The thin steps ARE the differentiation** — no separate “lower” worksheet; everyone climbs the same grade-level staircase as far as they can.
**Let groups borrow** from nearby boards — struggling groups get a peer scaffold without the teacher hovering.
**Watch the early slices** to catch access issues (a vocabulary word, a notation) before they compound.

blocks.text: Thin-slicing is the everyday workhorse of Core Instruction — the structure for building most procedural-conceptual skills through reasoning rather than demonstration. Pair it with rich tasks (for the big, open problems) and you have a complete task-based repertoire.
